::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Why are these vectors linearly dependent?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4146775/why-are-these-vectors-linearly-dependent), asked by [Ng Lok Chun](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/885039/ng-lok-chun) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2021-05-21; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I got it from [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_independence), but why are they dependent?
>
> [![three vectors in space.  One is a multiple of another, while the third has a different direction][q-1]][q-1]
>
>   [q-1]: oPGxX.png
>
> ([Image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_independence#/media/File:Vec-dep.png) by Wikimedia user Schnelliboy, cropped.  Used under a Creative Commons license ([CC-BY-SA-4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0))
:::

You see that two of the vectors are parallel—lying one on top of the other.  Call the shorter one $v_1$ and the longer one $v_2$.  Call the other one $v_3$.

Since $v_2$ and $v_1$ are parallel, there exists a scalar  $\lambda$ such that $v_2 = \lambda v_1$.  From the picture, it appears $\lambda \approx 1.5$.

Let $c_1 = \lambda$, $c_2 = -1$, and $c_3 = 0$.  These three scalars are not all zero.  Yet
$$c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2 + c_3 v_3 = 
   \lambda v_1 - v_2 + \vec 0 = \vec 0$$
So the three vectors $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ are linearly dependent.
